◇ Note. The completion formula. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest deliberate echoes of Gen 2:1–3: "thus the heavens and the earth were finished" — the same Hebrew root kalah ("complete") and the same liturgical cadence. The intertextual signal is precise: the construction of the tabernacle is presented as a creation-act parallel to the creation of the cosmos. The same parallel runs through the entire creation/tabernacle architecture: God creates in seven days; the tabernacle instructions come in seven divine speeches (Exod 25:1, 30:11, 30:17, 30:22, 30:34, 31:1, 31:12); creation culminates in Sabbath rest, and tabernacle instructions end with Sabbath command (31:12–17). The structural parallel encodes one of the OT’s deepest theological claims: the tabernacle is microcosm. Where Eden was the original meeting-place between God and humanity (Gen 3:8) and was lost, the tabernacle is the engineered restoration of that meeting-place at micro-scale. The verse is the formal closure of that creation-restoration narrative arc.

◇ Note. The high priest’s ephod. The ephod — a sleeveless apron-like vestment of gold thread woven with blue, purple, and scarlet — is one of the most enigmatic objects in OT cult. Its function is not just decorative: the ephod holds the breastpiece (28:15–30) with its twelve tribal stones and the Urim and Thummim (28:30, the oracular stones), making it the priestly oracular vestment proper. David twice uses an ephod for divine consultation (1 Sam 23:9, 30:7). In post-monarchic narratives, ephods proliferate problematically: Gideon makes an unauthorized ephod that becomes a snare (Judg 8:27), Micah’s shrine has one (Judg 17:5, 18:14–20). The legitimate Aaronide ephod is precisely calibrated; the unauthorized lay ephods that proliferate are precisely the cultic decay the deuteronomistic editor critiques. The verse is the institutional foundation for one of the OT’s clearest cases of a single object whose legitimate and illegitimate uses run through the entire historical narrative.

⌘ Hebrew. Ruaḥ Elohim (רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים) on the artist. Bezalel is the first individual in the OT explicitly described as "filled with the Spirit of God" — language that elsewhere in the OT attaches to prophets (Num 11:25 of the seventy elders), judges (Judg 3:10, Othniel), kings (1 Sam 10:10, Saul; 16:13, David), and rulers (Joseph, Gen 41:38). The use of the formula for an artist — for craft skill specifically — is unique to this chapter (with parallel at 35:31). The principle the verses introduce is theologically remarkable: artistic-craftsmanship is itself a charismatic gift on the same vocabulary footing as prophetic inspiration or kingly anointing. Jewish tradition (b. Berakhot 55a) develops this into the conviction that Bezalel possessed cosmic-architectural knowledge by Spirit-inspiration; Christian tradition (Augustine, Aquinas, and modern theologians of art like Dorothy Sayers) draws on the verse for theological aesthetics. Few OT passages so directly elevate craft and skilled labor to spiritual-vocational status.

◇ Note. The golden calf. Bull-imagery for high gods was widespread in the ANE — El at Ugarit was titled "Bull El," and bull-iconography accompanied Hadad/Baal across Canaan and Egypt’s Apis. Aaron’s declaration "These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (32:4) and his proclamation of "a feast to Yahweh" the next day (32:5) suggest the calf was meant as a Yahwistic image, not an alternative deity — a violation of the second commandment (image of Yahweh) rather than the first (other gods). The episode’s structural placement is devastating: the people violate the first principle of the just-given covenant while Moses is still on the mountain receiving the rest of it. Jeroboam’s later golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kgs 12:28) deliberately echo this episode, with the same proclamation almost word-for-word — registering the deuteronomistic editor’s judgment that Jeroboam reproduces Aaron’s sin at the institutional founding of the northern kingdom. The chapter is the foundational anti-syncretist text in the entire OT.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

The plate of pure gold on the high priest's forehead, engraved 'Holiness to the Lord' — Ephrem reads this as the priestly title borne by the high priest in figure and by Christ in fulfilment: the True Priest carries the holiness of the Lord on his very person, not as an ornament but as his essence. Tewahedo priestly vestments retain the canonical pattern of the Aaronic mitre as a deliberate iconographic echo.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (363). Ephrem the Syrian Sermo de Domino Nostro (c. 363 AD)

'There shall no man see me and live' — and yet Moses sees the Lord's back as he passes by. Ephrem reads the verse as the canonical disclosure that full vision of God is reserved for the Incarnation: only when the Word is made flesh may humanity behold the divine face without being consumed. Tewahedo reads Ex 33:20 and 1 Jn 1:1 ('which we have seen with our eyes') as a single canonical arc from veiled vision to face-to-face Word.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.14 (c. 350 AD)

'And he said, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live' — Athanasius marks ou dynēsē idein mou to prosōpon (thou canst not see my face) as the UNSEEABLE-FATHER / VISIBLE-WORD distinction. The Father-in-his-essence is unseeable (1 Tim 6:16 oude idein tis dynatai); what Moses is granted to see (LXX ta opisthia — 'the back parts') is the visible-condescension of the Word-pre-incarnate. Athanasius reads the Word as the agent of EVERY OT theophany (the burning bush, the pillar of cloud, the man-Yahweh at Mamre, the Sinai-glory) — the Father is never seen, only the Word who is the Father's-form-and-image. This hermeneutic grounds the Tewahedo iconographic-convention: the Father is never directly-depicted, only the Word-incarnate.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Moses descends with face shining and must put on a veil that the people may bear his presence. Paul reads the veil as the figure of the obscurity that remains over the OT until Christ takes it away (2 Cor 3:13-16). Ephrem follows Paul and reads Ex 34:30 as the canonical anchor of the veiled-to-unveiled progression: in the OT the prophet's borrowed glory must be covered; in the NT the believer beholds the Lord's own glory unveiled.

epub:type="footnote">

◇ Note. "Face to face." The phrase panim el panim ("face to face") is the OT’s most intimate idiom for divine encounter, applied here to Moses and to no one else in the Pentateuch except in retrospective summaries (Deut 34:10, "no prophet has arisen since in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face"). The phrase stands in productive tension with 33:20 ("you cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live") just verses later — the same chapter that asserts "face to face" intimacy denies that any human can survive seeing Yahweh’s face. Most readers (so Childs, Brueggemann) take the apparent contradiction as deliberate: "face to face" describes the unmediated quality of communication, not literal visual experience. Paul’s eschatological hope at 1 Cor 13:12 ("now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face") draws on this Mosaic framework — direct, unmediated knowledge as the eschatological promise. The verse is the OT’s definitive prophetic-paradigm formulation, against which all other prophetic experience is measured.

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:1.

Καὶ λήψῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐλαίου τῆς χρίσεως, καὶ ῥανεῖς ἐπὶ Ἀαρὼν καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν στολὴν αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς στολὰς τῶν υἱῶν αὐτοῦ μετʼ αὐτοῦ· καὶ ἁγιασθήσεται αὐτὸς καὶ ἡ στολὴ αὐτοῦ, καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ αἱ στολαὶ τῶν υἱῶν αὐτοῦ μετʼ αὐτοῦ· τὸ δὲ αἷμα τοῦ κριοῦ προσχεεῖς πρὸς τὸ θυσιαστήριον κύκλῳ.

↩

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 29:22.

Also thou shalt take of the ram the fat and the rump, and the fat that covereth the inwards, and the caul [above] the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat that [is] upon them, and the right shoulder; for it [is] a ram of consecration:

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְלָקַחְתָּ֣ מִן־הָ֠אַיִל הַחֵ֨לֶב וְהָֽאַלְיָ֜ה וְאֶת־הַחֵ֣לֶב ׀ הַֽמְכַסֶּ֣ה אֶת־הַקֶּ֗רֶב וְאֵ֨ת יֹתֶ֤רֶת הַכָּבֵד֙ וְאֵ֣ת ׀ שְׁתֵּ֣י הַכְּלָיֹ֗ת וְאֶת־הַחֵ֙לֶב֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עֲלֵהֶ֔ן וְאֵ֖ת שׁ֣וֹק הַיָּמִ֑ין כִּ֛י אֵ֥יל מִלֻּאִ֖ים הֽוּא׃

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

Καὶ λήψῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ κριοῦ τὸ στέαρ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὸ στέαρ τὸ κατακαλύπτον τὴν κοιλίαν, καὶ τὸν λοβὸν τοῦ ἥπατος, καὶ τοὺς δύο νεφροὺς, καὶ τὸ στέαρ τὸ ἐπʼ αὐτῶν, καὶ τὸν βραχίονα τὸν δεξιόν· ἔστι γὰρ τελείωσις αὕτη.

↩

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 29:23.

And one loaf of bread, and one cake of oiled bread, and one wafer out of the basket of the unleavened bread that [is] before the LORD:

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְכִכַּ֨ר לֶ֜חֶם אַחַ֗ת וַֽחַלַּ֨ת לֶ֥חֶם שֶׁ֛מֶן אַחַ֖ת וְרָקִ֣יק אֶחָ֑ד מִסַּל֙ הַמַּצּ֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֖ר לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

Καὶ ἄρτον ἕνα ἐξ ἐλαίου, καὶ λάγανον ἓν ἀπὸ τοῦ κανοῦ τῶν ἀζύμων τῶν προτεθειμένων ἔναντι Κυρίου.

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 29:24.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 29:25.

וְלָקַחְתָּ֤ אֹתָם֙ מִיָּדָ֔ם וְהִקְטַרְתָּ֥ הַמִּזְבֵּ֖חָה עַל־הָעֹלָ֑ה לְרֵ֤יחַ נִיח֙וֹחַ֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה אִשֶּׁ֥ה ה֖וּא לַיהוָֽה׃

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

Καὶ λήψῃ αὐτὰ ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτῶν, καὶ ἀνοίσεις ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον τῆς ὁλοκαυτώσεως εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας ἔναντι Κύριου· κάρπωμά ἐστι Κυρίῳ.

↩

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 29:26.

And thou shalt take the breast of the ram of Aaron’s consecration, and wave it [for] a wave offering before the LORD: and it shall be thy part.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְלָקַחְתָּ֣ אֶת־הֶֽחָזֶ֗ה מֵאֵ֤יל הַמִּלֻּאִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְאַהֲרֹ֔ן וְהֵנַפְתָּ֥ אֹת֛וֹ תְּנוּפָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וְהָיָ֥ה לְךָ֖ לְמָנָֽה׃

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 29:27.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְקִדַּשְׁתָּ֞ אֵ֣ת ׀ חֲזֵ֣ה הַתְּנוּפָ֗ה וְאֵת֙ שׁ֣וֹק הַתְּרוּמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר הוּנַ֖ף וַאֲשֶׁ֣ר הוּרָ֑ם מֵאֵיל֙ הַמִּלֻּאִ֔ים מֵאֲשֶׁ֥ר לְאַהֲרֹ֖ן וּמֵאֲשֶׁ֥ר לְבָנָֽיו׃

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 29:28.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְהָיָה֩ לְאַהֲרֹ֨ן וּלְבָנָ֜יו לְחָק־עוֹלָ֗ם מֵאֵת֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּ֥י תְרוּמָ֖ה ה֑וּא וּתְרוּמָ֞ה יִהְיֶ֨ה מֵאֵ֤ת בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מִזִּבְחֵ֣י שַׁלְמֵיהֶ֔ם תְּרוּמָתָ֖ם לַיהוָֽה׃

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)
